screens.title: Character Movement and Controllers
screens.subtitle: Choosing and implementing the right movement method: Rigidbody, Transform, or CharacterController

narration.text: In this chapter we will compare three core ways to move characters in Unity and learn when to choose each. You will understand Rigidbody-based motion for full physics interactions, Transform-based motion for simple, non-physics movement, and the CharacterController for collision-aware, non-physics control. We'll examine walking, running, jumping, and dashing patterns and the practical issues that commonly appear, like sticky movement, sliding, and floating after a jump. You will see concrete examples of Rigidbody AddForce and velocity control, Transform. Translate for simple moves, and the CharacterController Move approach with manual gravity. Throughout, I will highlight small but important rules: use FixedUpdate with Rigidbody, use Time. deltaTime with Update-based movement, and never put a Rigidbody and a CharacterController on the same GameObject. By the end you'll be able to pick the right controller type for a platformer, a pushable physics object, or a precisely controlled cinematic character, and you'll know the common fixes when movement feels wrong. Think about a single player that needs to be pushed by wind zones and also jump precisely — this chapter will show why a physics Rigidbody is often the correct starting point.

keyIdea.title: Core insight
keyIdea.text: Match your movement method to the gameplay requirements: physics interaction needs Rigidbody, precise script control can use Transform, and collision-focused player control fits CharacterController.

screens.title: Learning Objectives
screens.subtitle: Skills you'll practice and why they matter

narration.text: These four objectives guide your hands-on practice and understanding of character movement. First, you will implement Rigidbody-based movement using AddForce, MovePosition, and velocity adjustments so your character interacts properly with physics and other rigid bodies. Practically, this matters when your player must push crates or be affected by wind forces. Second, you'll understand when Transform-based movement is appropriate: for UI elements, cinematic motion, or objects that do not participate in physics. This helps you avoid accidental collision bypasses. Third, you'll use Unity's CharacterController to implement collision-aware, non-physics movement with manual gravity and jumping. This is the common choice for precise player control in many games. Fourth, you'll develop walking, running, jumping, and dashing patterns and learn to diagnose issues like sliding, sticky movement, or floating jumps. Each objective has a direct milestone: implement the feature, verify its behavior, and fix the common mistakes. Knowing these skills improves gameplay feel, reduces physics bugs, and makes your movement code predictable across frame rates.

keyIdea.title: Verified milestone
keyIdea.text: Be able to implement and compare Rigidbody and CharacterController movement, and fix at least two common movement bugs.

screens.title: Practice and checks
screens.subtitle: What you will implement and validate in the hands-on activity

narration.text: This second objectives slide focuses on concrete checkpoints you will use while building the hands-on scene. Start by creating two characters: one with a Rigidbody and one with a CharacterController. For the Rigidbody character, validate that forces and velocity changes produce realistic pushes and that MovePosition respects collisions when called in FixedUpdate. For the CharacterController, confirm controller. isGrounded behavior and that manual gravity causes the character to land reliably. Measure jumping: the Rigidbody should use an impulse force, while the CharacterController requires computing an initial upward velocity based on the desired jump height and your custom gravity. Also, test control consistency across frame rates by toggling frame limits and observing whether motion remains stable. Finally, reproduce at least two movement bugs intentionally—sliding due to low drag, and floating caused by missing gravity—and fix them. These validation steps teach you both correct implementation and the debugging patterns you will rely on in real projects.

keyIdea.title: Practice tip
keyIdea.text: Implement both controllers in the same scene and use the same input to compare how each responds to identical commands.

Implementation Checklist
Four validation checks to complete during your lab.
Rigidbody checks
  • Call MovePosition or set velocity in FixedUpdate to avoid jitter.
  • Preserve vertical velocity when setting rb.velocity to keep gravity working.
  • Adjust drag or PhysicMaterial to prevent sliding.

Gameplay checks

  • Test jumping across different frame rates for consistency.
Debug targets
  • Fix sliding with drag or PhysicMaterial adjustments.
  • Fix floating with explicit gravity application for CharacterController.

screens.title: Rigidbody-based movement
screens.subtitle: Why and how to use physics-driven motion

narration.text: Rigidbody-based movement means using Unity's physics body to determine motion through forces, impulses, or setting velocity directly. Use it when the character must fully participate in the physics simulation: being pushed by objects, reacting to wind, or colliding naturally with dynamic world geometry. The defining claim is that a Rigidbody lets Unity resolve collisions and motion together, so your character behaves like any other physics object. A common concrete example is a player that can push crates and be knocked back by explosions: applying an impulse keeps interactions realistic. When implementing Rigidbody movement, call physics changes inside FixedUpdate so they synchronize with the physics timestep; otherwise you will see jitter. A common misconception is that you should never set velocity directly. In fact, carefully setting rb. velocity is a valid pattern for tight control, but you must preserve the vertical component when you want gravity and jumps to continue working. Key checks: set appropriate drag and use PhysicMaterial on ground surfaces to avoid infinite sliding, and use MovePosition for deterministic, collision-aware repositioning when you need precise interpolation. Ask yourself: does the character need to be pushed or feel forces? If yes, Rigidbody is the correct path.

keyIdea.title: Why Rigidbody?
keyIdea.text: Use Rigidbody when characters must interact naturally with physics forces and other dynamic objects.

content.html:
Module 3 › Chapter 3.3 › Rigidbody-based movement
Rigidbody movement explained
For characters that should respond to forces and push other physics bodies.
Primary APIs
Apply AddForce for impulses, set rb.velocity for direct control, or use MovePosition for interpolation that still respects collisions.
Bulleted tips
  • Call physics changes in FixedUpdate to match the physics timestep.
  • Preserve rb.velocity.y when modifying velocity so gravity keeps working.
  • Adjust drag or PhysicMaterial to control sliding on surfaces.
Example scenario
A player uses an impulse to jump and later is pushed by a moving crate; both interactions use rigidbody forces for natural motion.
Key Takeaway

Rigidbody movement integrates with the physics engine—use it when forces and realistic interactions matter.

Visual: Movement patterns
Impulse Jump
Use AddForce with an impulse Mode for single jumps.
Smooth MovePosition
MovePosition interpolates while still allowing collision resolution; call inside FixedUpdate.
Common mistake
Setting transform.position on a Rigidbody causes unstable physics and jitter.

screens.title: AddForce, velocity, and MovePosition
screens.subtitle: Choosing the right Rigidbody method and timing

narration.text: When using a Rigidbody there are three common ways to drive motion: applying forces with AddForce, setting or lerping rb. velocity, and using MovePosition to interpolate a position while preserving collision resolution. Each method has a trade-off. AddForce is best when you want the physics engine to calculate acceleration, drag, and interactions with other forces. Use it for punchy impulses or continuous thrust. Setting rb. velocity directly gives deterministic control over speed; it is useful for tight player-feel movement but requires you to preserve vertical velocity if gravity should remain active. MovePosition is ideal when you want collision-aware, smooth repositioning — it avoids teleport-like collisions and is often used for kinematic-like behavior while still interacting properly. Always make these changes in FixedUpdate so physics updates stay synchronized; doing so in Update will produce inconsistent results across frame rates. A concrete example: compute a target horizontal velocity from input, copy current rb. velocity. y into the target, then lerp rb. velocity toward the target using an acceleration factor multiplied by Time. fixedDeltaTime. Misconception to avoid: using transform. position updates on an object with a Rigidbody leads to conflict and jitter. The closing question: when do you prefer deterministic velocity control over additive forces?

keyIdea.title: Method match
keyIdea.text: Pick AddForce for natural physics, velocity for tight deterministic control, and MovePosition for smooth collision-aware interpolation.

content.html:
Module 3 › Chapter 3.3 › Rigidbody methods
When to use each method
Practical patterns and a pseudo-code walkthrough to show timing and data flow.
AddForce
Use for impulses and continuous forces where physics should determine acceleration and collisions.
Velocity control
Set or lerp rb.velocity for precise horizontal speeds. Preserve vertical component to keep gravity intact.
MovePosition
Interpolate the Rigidbody smoothly while still allowing collision resolution; call from FixedUpdate.
Key Takeaway

Synchronize Rigidbody work with FixedUpdate and select the method that balances realism and control for your game feel.

Pseudo-code walkthrough
// In FixedUpdate:
// compute target horizontal velocity from input
// preserve rb.velocity.y before applying
// rb.velocity = Vector3.Lerp(rb.velocity, targetVelocity, accel * Time.fixedDeltaTime)
// For jump: rb.AddForce(up * jumpForce, impulse)
Common mistake
Calling MovePosition or velocity changes in Update can produce inconsistent collision responses across frame rates.
Pro tip
Use small drag values and PhysicMaterials on surfaces to tune how quickly a body stops instead of forcing velocity to zero abruptly.

screens.title: Transform-based movement
screens.subtitle: Fast direct motion and when it breaks down

narration.text: Transform-based movement is the simplest approach: you directly change an object's position each frame, using methods like transform. Translate or by modifying transform. position. This works well for objects that do not require collision response from the physics engine — for example, background parallax elements, UI panels, or cinematic characters that must follow a scripted path. The main advantage is simplicity and performance. The key limitation is that Transform updates bypass Unity's physics system: colliders passed through by Transform changes will not generate standard collision callbacks, and physics bodies will not be affected by that motion. An important example is moving a platform by updating its transform; a Rigidbody standing on that platform may not react as expected unless you write additional code. Misconceptions often arise when developers expect collisions to just happen; if you need collisions, you must implement raycasts or overlap checks yourself, or choose a CharacterController or Rigidbody. A practical test is to move an object and watch whether OnCollisionEnter is called. If it is not, you are using a Transform approach that does not trigger physics collision resolution. The takeaway: use Transform for simple, non-physics movement, otherwise prefer a physics-aware method.

keyIdea.title: Transform trade-off
keyIdea.text: Use Transform for simple scripted motion; avoid it when collision response or physics interaction is required.

content.html:
Module 3 › Chapter 3.3 › Transform movement
Direct transform motion
Fast and simple but not physics-aware.
Use cases
Background scrolling, UI panels, or tightly scripted cinematic movement without physics.
Limitations
Transform updates ignore physics collisions and will not trigger OnCollisionEnter or natural responses from physics objects.
Developer check
If your moving object must push or be pushed, prefer Rigidbody or implement raycasts and overlap checks in your script.
Key Takeaway

Transform motion is efficient but bypasses collision physics—choose it only when you control interactions explicitly.

Example scenario
A cinematic camera dolly that follows a spline should use Transform updates for exact positioning. If that dolly needs to push physics objects, redesign it as a kinematic Rigidbody and use MovePosition instead.
Common mistake
Expecting OnCollisionEnter callbacks from transform-controlled motion; they won't happen without explicit physics queries.
Pro tip
If you need both precise position and collision response, consider a kinematic Rigidbody and MovePosition called in FixedUpdate.

narration.text: The CharacterController is a specialized component that provides a capsule-shaped collider and built-in collision resolution but does not use the physics engine to apply forces. Instead, you explicitly move the controller by calling its Move method with a displacement vector. This gives you collision-aware motion and sliding along walls without the complications of a Rigidbody. Because it doesn't use physics gravity, you must implement vertical motion yourself: maintain a playerVelocity. y variable, apply gravity each frame, and pass the combined horizontal and vertical displacements to Move. A concrete example is a first-person controller that requires precise strafe and look controls but still needs to collide with world geometry; using CharacterController. Move yields smooth collision handling and automatic slide behavior. A common misconception is to assume OnCollisionEnter works; instead use OnControllerColliderHit for collision callbacks specific to the CharacterController. Another important rule is to call controller. Move in Update when you manage input and use Time. deltaTime to make motion frame-rate independent. The takeaway: CharacterController is the best fit when you want collision handling and tight programmatic control without full physics forces.

keyIdea.title: Controller core
keyIdea.text: CharacterController provides collision handling and sliding without Rigidbody physics; you must supply gravity and vertical motion.

content.html:
Module 3 › Chapter 3.3 › CharacterController
How CharacterController works
It handles collisions and sliding but not physics forces; you drive motion directly.
Move() API
Pass a displacement vector to Move. The controller attempts to move, slides along colliders, and updates isGrounded for you.
Vertical motion
Maintain playerVelocity.y and apply gravity each Update. Reset the vertical velocity when isGrounded and the value is negative.
Collision callbacks
Use OnControllerColliderHit for controller-specific collision events; OnCollisionEnter will not fire for the controller itself.
Key Takeaway

CharacterController is ideal for responsive, collision-aware player movement when you do not need physics forces.

Example: manual gravity flow
Compute horizontal movement from input, call controller.Move(horizontal * speed * deltaTime), update playerVelocity.y with gravity, and call controller.Move(playerVelocity * deltaTime) for vertical displacement.
Common mistake
Forgetting to reset playerVelocity.y when grounded causes accumulating negative velocity or inconsistent jumps.
Pro tip
Use controller.isGrounded for a quick ground check, and add a small downward offset when necessary for steeper slopes.

screens.title: Implementing walking and running
screens.subtitle: Patterns for Rigidbody and CharacterController movement

narration.text: Walking and running are fundamentally about scaling a horizontal movement vector. For a Rigidbody-driven character compute a target velocity from input and desired move speed, preserve the y component for gravity, and either set rb. velocity or apply forces that accelerate toward that velocity. Smooth changes use a lerp between current and target velocity using an acceleration factor multiplied by Time. fixedDeltaTime. For a CharacterController, compute a horizontal Vector3 using the character's facing and input, then call controller. Move(move * moveSpeed * Time. deltaTime). Running is simply a speed multiplier applied to the same vector. A concrete example: a Rigidbody player calculates a normalized move direction, multiplies by moveSpeed, sets targetVelocity. y to rb. velocity. y, and then lerps rb. velocity toward targetVelocity inside FixedUpdate. A common misconception is that identical input should produce identical feel across systems; in practice, physics introduces momentum and drag, while CharacterController provides immediate, stiff responses. When tuning, watch acceleration rate, drag, and ground friction. A closing question: which method gives more immediate control for tight platformers, and why? The answer leans toward CharacterController or velocity-setting Rigidbody patterns because they let you precisely cap and control horizontal speed.

keyIdea.title: Walk/Run pattern
keyIdea.text: Compute horizontal move vector from input and apply it via velocity or Move()—use multipliers to switch between walk and run.

content.html:
Module 3 › Chapter 3.3 › Walking & Running
Rigidbody pattern
Compute target velocity and lerp rb.velocity in FixedUpdate.
Steps
  1. Get normalized input direction.
  2. targetVelocity = direction * moveSpeed; targetVelocity.y = rb.velocity.y
  3. Lerp rb.velocity towards targetVelocity using acceleration * Time.fixedDeltaTime.
Tuning
Adjust accelerationFactor for responsiveness and drag for natural slow-down.
CharacterController pattern
Compute horizontal move and call Move() with Time.deltaTime scaling.
Steps
  1. Read input and build horizontal move vector relative to facing.
  2. controller.Move(move * moveSpeed * Time.deltaTime).
  3. Apply playerVelocity.y vertical motion with controller.Move(playerVelocity * Time.deltaTime).
Tuning
Use run multipliers, and clamp maximum horizontal speed to keep consistent feel.
Common misconception
Assuming physics will make movement feel better; sometimes deterministic control gives clearer, more responsive gameplay.

screens.title: Jumping and dashing
screens.subtitle: Vertical impulses and short bursts of speed

narration.text: Jumping has two common implementations depending on your controller choice. For a Rigidbody character apply an impulse upward using AddForce with an impulse ForceMode so the physics engine computes the resulting arc. Preserve the horizontal velocity components and only change the vertical impulse. For a CharacterController, calculate the necessary initial upward velocity from the desired jump height and your custom gravity value using the square root formula. Add that value to your playerVelocity. y and let gravity reduce it over time. Dashing is a short, high-speed movement. For Rigidbody players apply a VelocityChange or a brief strong force in the dash direction; for CharacterController players move the controller quickly along the dash vector for a short duration. A common mistake is allowing repeated jumps because of unreliable ground checks. Use controller. isGrounded for the CharacterController and OnCollisionEnter/Physics. Raycast or a dedicated ground flag for Rigidbody players. Also be mindful of mixing Time. deltaTime and Time. fixedDeltaTime: jumps and dashes should be calculated in the appropriate update loop. Final takeaway: treat vertical motion separately from horizontal motion and ensure your ground checks prevent multiple unintended jumps.

keyIdea.title: Jump vs Dash
keyIdea.text: Jumping modifies vertical velocity or adds an impulse; dashing temporarily boosts horizontal speed—implement ground checks to avoid repeats.

content.html:
Module 3 › Chapter 3.3 › Jumping & Dashing
Jump implementations
Two patterns depending on controller type.
Rigidbody jump
Apply AddForce upward with impulse mode. Keep horizontal velocity untouched to preserve momentum.
CharacterController jump
Calculate initial vertical velocity from desired height and gravity, add to playerVelocity.y, then apply gravity each Update.
Ground checks
Use controller.isGrounded for CharacterController and collision or raycast checks for Rigidbody to prevent double jumps.
Dashing
Short bursts of speed applied horizontally.
Rigidbody dash
Apply a quick AddForce with ForceMode.VelocityChange or set velocity for a single frame to achieve a crisp dash.
CharacterController dash
Temporarily add a strong horizontal displacement to the Move call for a brief duration; clamp collisions as necessary.
Common mistake
Allowing dash and jump without proper state gating causes unintended movement stacks; gate actions behind grounded or cooldown checks.

screens.title: Common pitfalls and fixes
screens.subtitle: Sticky movement, sliding, floating jumps, and mis-synced updates

narration.text: Many movement bugs arise from a few recurring causes. Sticky movement often comes from incorrect reseting of vertical velocity or poor ground checks — for example, forgetting to zero the vertical component on a CharacterController when grounded leads to small upward velocities that impede movement. Sliding occurs when Rigidbodies have too little drag or the ground PhysicMaterial has low friction; the fix is to increase drag or add friction to the ground material, or to apply counter forces. Floating jumps commonly happen when developers forget to implement manual gravity for CharacterController-based motion. Always apply gravity each Update and reset vertical velocity on landing. A subtle but critical mistake is mixing Update and FixedUpdate incorrectly: call physics modifications in FixedUpdate and frame-based movement in Update. For ground checking, rely on controller. isGrounded where possible, and use Raycast or collision callbacks for Rigidbody players. Another pitfall is combining Rigidbody and CharacterController on the same GameObject — they conflict and produce unpredictable results. The closing question: what two checks will you add first when diagnosing a strange movement feeling? Start with which update loop your code runs in and whether gravity is applied.

keyIdea.title: Debug checklist
keyIdea.text: When movement feels wrong, verify update loop placement, ground checks, gravity handling, and physics material or drag settings.

content.html:
Module 3 › Chapter 3.3 › Pitfalls & Fixes
Common issues and how to fix them
Sticky movement
Reset vertical velocity when grounded and ensure ground checks are reliable.
Sliding
Increase Rigidbody drag or use PhysicMaterials with friction to stop indefinite sliding.
Floating jumps
Implement manual gravity for CharacterController and apply it every Update.
Update loop mismatch
Use FixedUpdate for physics and Update for input-driven Move calls; mixing causes inconsistent behavior.
Mixing controllers
Never place a Rigidbody and CharacterController on the same GameObject; choose one approach per actor.
Quick diagnostic
Ask: which update loop? is gravity applied? is ground check reliable? These reveal most issues quickly.

screens.title: Ground checking strategies
screens.subtitle: Reliable checks for jumping and landing

narration.text: A reliable ground check is essential for preventing double jumps and for resetting vertical motion. For CharacterController you can usually rely on controller. isGrounded, which Unity sets after Move. If you need more control, perform a short downward raycast or a sphere cast from the character's feet to the ground within a small distance threshold. For Rigidbody characters OnCollisionEnter/OnCollisionStay tied to a ground tag is a common pattern, and many developers also use a short downward raycast as a secondary validation to handle edge cases like moving platforms or small gaps. A concrete example: cast a ray from a point slightly above the character's feet down a small distance equal to groundCheckDistance and confirm the hit collides with objects tagged as ground. Misconceptions include relying solely on contact normals from collisions; while useful, collision callbacks can miss quick contacts on fast-moving objects. Always choose a ground check tuned to your movement speed. The closing practical tip: when your player sometimes can't jump after a short hop, widen the ground check slightly or perform both a raycast and a collision flag to increase reliability without causing false positives.

keyIdea.title: Ground check
keyIdea.text: Use controller.isGrounded for basic cases, and add raycasts or collision flags for robust ground detection across moving platforms and fast motion.

content.html:
Module 3 › Chapter 3.3 › Ground Checking
Ground check patterns
Choose a method that matches your movement speed and environment complexity.
controller.isGrounded
Simple and built-in for CharacterController; reliable after Move() updates.
Raycast
Cast a short ray downward from the feet; tune distance to avoid false positives on slopes.
Collision callbacks
Use OnCollisionEnter/Stay for Rigidbody players and check contact tags or normals for ground detection.
Practical tip
Combine a short raycast with controller.isGrounded or collision flags to handle moving platforms and quick hops robustly.
Pitfall
Too-large raycasts pick up distant geometry and create false grounded states; tune distances conservatively.
Key Takeaway
Reliable ground checks prevent unintended double jumps and ensure consistent landing behavior.

screens.title: Lab walkthrough: two players in one scene
screens.subtitle: Set up, scripts, and what to observe

narration.text: In the hands-on lab you'll create two cubes: one with a Rigidbody and one with a CharacterController. Attach a Rigidbody component to the first and a CharacterController to the second. For the Rigidbody player, implement input capture in Update, call AddForce for jumps or set rb. velocity inside FixedUpdate for movement, and use OnCollisionEnter to set a grounded flag. For the CharacterController player, attach a script that computes horizontal movement with controller. Move, maintains playerVelocity. y, applies gravity each Update, and uses controller. isGrounded to reset vertical velocity. Assign different input schemes or run both with the same axes to compare behavior. Run the scene and watch: the Rigidbody player will be affected by external forces and will push other rigid bodies, while the CharacterController will slide along geometry and not be pushed by physics without explicit code in OnControllerColliderHit. Introduce a wind zone or moving crate to observe differences. Fix any sliding by adding drag or PhysicMaterial, and correct floating by ensuring manual gravity is applied each frame. After testing, reflect: which player felt more responsive for platforming and which behaved more naturally when interacting with physics objects?

keyIdea.title: Lab aim
keyIdea.text: Compare feel and interaction by running both controllers with the same input and environment, then iterate on tuning.

content.html:
Module 3 › Chapter 3.3 › Lab walkthrough
Hands-on: Rigidbody vs CharacterController
Step-by-step setup and what to observe in runtime.
Setup
  • Create a Ground plane tagged Ground.
  • Create two Cubes: one named PlayerRigidbody with a Rigidbody, one named PlayerCharacterController with a CharacterController.
  • Attach the respective scripts and tune Height/Radius on the controller.
What to test
  • Compare jump arcs and landing behavior.
  • Observe pushing interactions with crates and wind forces.
  • Intentionally cause sliding and floating and fix them.
Observation
Rigidbody reacts to forces and pushes objects; CharacterController handles collisions but needs explicit code to affect rigidbodies.
Key Takeaway
Running both in parallel is the fastest way to learn the differences and pick the right approach for your game.

screens.title: Tuning and performance
screens.subtitle: Friction, drag, acceleration, and stable frame-rate behavior

narration.text: Tuning movement is part science and part art. For Rigidbody characters balance drag and PhysicMaterial friction to control how quickly the character slows when input stops. For highly responsive control use a combination of velocity setting and small drag, rather than instant zeroing of velocity, which looks unnatural. Acceleration factors control how fast the character reaches target speed: low acceleration feels heavy, high acceleration feels snappy. For CharacterController, tune moveSpeed, sprint multipliers, and how you apply gravity so the vertical motion matches horizontal responsiveness. Performance-wise, avoid heavy per-frame physics queries like many overlapping sphere checks; prefer a single short raycast or the built-in isGrounded where possible. Also, ensure you use Time. fixedDeltaTime in FixedUpdate so physics behavior stays stable across frame rate changes. A common misconception is that higher physics timesteps always make movement smoother; while they can reduce jitter, they also increase C P U cost — instead, keep physics stable and tune factors for perceived feel. Final thought: tune with playtesting and small iterative changes, testing across frame rates and different platform builds when possible. Tuning and performance means tune acceleration and drag for feel, use physicmaterials for friction, and keep physics code in fixedupdate for stable behavior.. In practical terms, friction, drag, acceleration, and stable frame-rate behavior. A concrete example makes the pattern visible, and a brief contrast helps prevent a common misconception. This matters because learners need the underlying reasoning before they can apply the idea confidently or notice where it breaks down. The main takeaway is that the concept should be understood as a meaningful pattern, not just a label on the screen.

keyIdea.title: Tuning tip
keyIdea.text: Tune acceleration and drag for feel, use PhysicMaterials for friction, and keep physics code in FixedUpdate for stable behavior.

content.html:
Module 3 › Chapter 3.3 › Tuning & Performance
Tune for feel, not just numbers
Small parameter changes can meaningfully alter perceived responsiveness.
Drag & friction
Use Rigidbody drag and PhysicMaterials to control slide and stopping behavior rather than clamping velocities abruptly.
Acceleration
Acceleration factor determines how quickly you approach target speed. Tune it with the intended game feel in mind.
Frame-rate stability
Keep physics updates in FixedUpdate and scale movements with the appropriate delta time to avoid inconsistent behavior across frame rates.
Performance tip
Prefer a single raycast or contact flag for ground checks rather than many overlapping geometry queries every frame.
Playtest loop
Iterate with small changes and test across platforms to ensure movement feels consistent and performant.
Key Takeaway
Tune physics and controller parameters iteratively; subtle adjustments often produce the best improvements in feel.

screens.title: Key Concepts
screens.subtitle: Three essential ideas from this chapter

narration.text: Let's summarize three core ideas to remember. First: Rigidbody-based movement uses forces, velocity, or MovePosition and should be updated in FixedUpdate for stable physics interactions. Use it when the character must be pushed or affected by environmental physics. Second: Transform-based movement updates positions directly and is fast for non-physics objects, but it bypasses collision detection and requires custom raycasts if collisions matter. Third: CharacterController. Move provides collision-aware movement without a Rigidbody, so you must implement manual gravity and use OnControllerColliderHit for controller-specific collisions. Keep these distinctions in mind when designing characters: they determine collision callbacks, interaction with forces, and how you implement jumps or dashes. A practical prompt: before implementing movement, list whether your character must be pushed, respond to forces, or require tight deterministic control. That simple question will point you to the right approach.

keyIdea.title: Three essentials
keyIdea.text: Match controller type to gameplay: physics interaction → Rigidbody, scripted precision → Transform, collision-aware player control → CharacterController.

content.html:
Module 3 › Chapter 3.3 › Key Concepts
Rigidbody Movement
Force, velocity, or MovePosition in FixedUpdate gives full physics interaction.
Transform Movement
Direct position updates are fast but ignore physics and collisions.
CharacterController
Collision-aware Move with manual gravity and controller-specific callbacks.
Summary

Choose the controller that best matches whether you need physics interactions, deterministic control, or collision-aware player movement.

screens.title: What to Remember
screens.subtitle: Three focused reminders for implementation and debugging

narration.text: A final set of compact reminders will help you implement movement reliably. First, always match the update loop to the movement method: FixedUpdate for Rigidbody physics and Update for CharacterController or Transform changes. Second, implement reliable ground checks using controller. isGrounded, raycasts, or collision flags so jumps and grounded resets are consistent. Third, avoid mixing Rigidbody and CharacterController on the same GameObject because they conflict. These checks prevent the most frequent movement bugs and lead to more predictable and tunable player feel. Before you finish a movement implementation, run tests for pushing objects, sliding, and jumping across a range of frame rates—small edge cases often reveal the best improvements. What single question will you ask when choosing a controller for your next character? Ask whether that character must react to external physics forces or simply needs precise scripted control.

keyIdea.title: Final reminder
keyIdea.text: Use the correct update loop, verify ground checks, and never combine conflicting controller components on a single object.

content.html:
Module 3 › Chapter 3.3 › Final Reminders
Update loops
FixedUpdate for physics, Update for frame-based motion and input.
Ground checks
Use isGrounded, raycasts, or collision flags tuned to your movement speed.
Component conflicts
Do not combine Rigidbody and CharacterController on the same GameObject.
Closing

Use these reminders as a quick checklist when you design and debug character movement to ensure consistent and predictable behavior.
